rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the gradient fixed and raise temperature to test selectivity changes in the crowded middle cluster and nearly coeluting final pair. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving time for a shallower gradient if needed.

Complete the temperature scout at the low endpoint while holding the gradient fixed. This tests whether cooling separates the critical cluster more effectively before committing injections to gradient refinement.

Cooling gave the best selectivity, so retain 25 C and make the gradient shallower to improve the two remaining critical pairs. The current last peak at 6.06 minutes provides room to increase separation without a time penalty.

The middle critical pair appears to reverse order as the gradient becomes shallower; go beyond that crossover to seek useful separation while retaining the improved late-pair resolution. Raise the starting organic fraction slightly to help keep the last peak within 10 minutes.
Slightly reduce the gradient slope to bring the remaining R = 1.40 pair above 1.5. The last peak at 9.25 minutes leaves a small time margin, making this a promising step toward CRF 1.0.

The maximum CRF is secured; now seek a shorter fully resolved method. Raising the starting organic fraction should advance elution, while the slope remains close to injection 6 to help preserve critical-pair resolution.

Lengthen the gradient by one step to recover the middle pair’s resolution while retaining the faster elution from the higher starting organic fraction. This should test whether full resolution can be restored with the last peak earlier than injection 6.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to shorten the elution window, paired with a shallower gradient to protect the marginal middle-pair resolution. Injection 8 remains the fastest fully resolved method demonstrated so far.

Raise temperature one step from the fastest fully resolved method to seek earlier elution without sacrificing resolution. This also tests temperature selectivity on the shallow-gradient side of the middle-pair crossover.

Apply the modest temperature increase to injection 9, whose wider early-pair spacing may tolerate warming better than injection 8. Warming may lift its R = 1.33 middle pair above 1.5 while shortening the elution window.

Make the gradient one step shallower to improve the sole unresolved pair at R = 1.30. Monitor the early and final pairs, which have limited resolution margin, while targeting full resolution in less time than injection 8.

Test whether further warming moves the early and late clusters beyond their selectivity crossovers under this shallow gradient. The maximum score is already secured, so this explores a potentially faster fully resolved temperature regime.

Raise temperature one step to move the nearly coeluting middle pair beyond its apparent crossover. Keep the gradient fixed to assess whether this restores full resolution while further shortening elution.

Test the high-temperature endpoint with the shallower gradient, seeking to move the late pair beyond its temperature-driven crossover and separate the middle cluster. This explores a faster alternative while retaining injection 8 as the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.

Lower the starting organic fraction at 45 C to alter selectivity in the two marginal pairs from injection 14. The seven-minute elution window leaves ample room to recover resolution while remaining faster than the current fully resolved method.

Test whether a shallower gradient at 45 C can resolve the two marginal pairs from injection 14. Keeping the starting composition fixed isolates the slope response, with room for some additional retention before reaching 10 minutes.

Return to the temperature that achieved full resolution and test a higher starting organic fraction with a substantially shallower gradient. This seeks a shorter elution window while compensating for the middle-pair resolution loss seen when the starting fraction was raised previously.

Test the steeper-gradient side of the middle-pair crossover at the higher starting organic fraction. This may recover middle-pair separation and substantially shorten elution, while checking whether the late pair retains adequate resolution.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention while modestly reducing the gradient slope, aiming to lift the late pair from R = 1.43 above 1.5. Monitor the middle cluster to ensure its existing resolution is preserved.

Lengthen the gradient one step to improve the two marginal pairs from injection 20. The middle pair on the other side has R = 2.19, providing some margin for the selectivity shift while targeting full resolution near four minutes.
Raise temperature one step from the new fastest fully resolved method to seek shorter retention. Keep the gradient fixed and check whether the middle cluster and late pair retain R >= 1.5.

Return to 25 C and test a higher starting organic fraction to advance elution, using a shallower gradient to compensate for the middle-pair resolution loss. Injection 21 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.

Test beyond the temperature-driven middle-pair crossover to seek full resolution with earlier elution than injection 21. The maximum CRF is already secured, so this final temperature exploration targets a faster alternative.

Preserve injection 21’s successful slope of 0.05 organic fraction per minute while shortening the programmed gradient to four minutes. The gradient endpoint reaches the outlet at 4.65 minutes, after its last peak at 4.14 minutes, so this should retain full resolution and CRF 1.0.
